title: Customer success
description: Judge how the change affects the health, adoption and renewal of existing customer accounts, and who follows each account up.
expertises: Account health scoring and renewal risk
questions: Which accounts does the change touch, and how would their health score move?
What will a customer success manager tell each affected account, and when?
Which usage, ticket or renewal signal would show that an account is at risk because of the change?

sources.title: Bain & Company, Measuring your Net Promoter Score
Consortium for Service Innovation, Knowledge-Centered Success (KCS)
Stripe, Billing analytics (MRR, churn and subscriber reports)

specialists.title: Account health analyst
specialists.focus: Define the health score inputs the change affects, such as active users, key feature use, tickets and survey answers, and check that each input has a source and a refresh date.
checks: Each health input names its system of record and the date it was last refreshed.
The score separates usage decline from seasonal patterns, such as holidays or fiscal year ends.
A red account has a named owner and an action due date, not only a colour.

specialists.title: Renewal manager
specialists.focus: List the renewals that fall inside the rollout window and judge whether the change raises the risk of a downgrade or a lost contract.
checks: Renewals in the next 90 days are listed with their value and owner before the change ships.
Contract clauses that the change could breach, such as a removed feature or a changed limit, are flagged to legal.
Churn is reported as both logo churn and revenue churn, with the formula written down.

specialists.title: Customer onboarding lead
specialists.focus: Check that new and existing accounts can reach first value with the change, and that the onboarding plan names the steps, owners and target dates.
checks: The time-to-first-value milestone is defined as an observable event, not a call booked.
Onboarding material shows the changed flow, with screenshots of the released version.
Accounts in onboarding during the release get a heads-up and an adjusted plan.

specialists.title: Voice of the customer lead
specialists.focus: Read survey answers, tickets and call notes for the area the change touches and separate what customers asked for from what the team assumes.
checks: NPS is computed as promoters (9-10) minus detractors (0-6) on the same question and population over time.
Verbatims cited in a decision carry their date and account segment.
Feedback from a single large account is labelled as such and not generalised to a segment.

evidence: Current health scores and their inputs for the accounts or segment the change affects.
Renewal calendar with contract value, renewal date and owner for those accounts.
Recent tickets, survey answers and call notes about the area the change touches, with dates.
Adoption data before the change and the metric the team will follow after it.
challenge: Which account would be the first to complain or downgrade, and has anyone told them?
Does the health score reflect real use of the product, or activity that looks good without delivering value?
Would a staged rollout by segment protect the renewals that fall in the next quarter?
Which commitments made in sales or QBR conversations does the change contradict?
decision_criteria: Proceed when affected accounts are identified, their owners briefed and the follow-up metric defined.
Revise when the change removes or limits something that renewing customers use, until the contract and communication impact is settled.
Ask for a staged rollout when renewals worth a material share of recurring revenue fall inside the rollout window.
Name the health signal and threshold that would trigger outreach to an account after release.
